question: How does PostgreSQL implement Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) without in-place updates? How does PostgreSQL implement Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) without in-place updates?

options.text: Every UPDATE writes a completely new tuple version to the heap page, populating xmin (creation transaction) and xmax (deletion transaction).
Every UPDATE locks the existing tuple and modifies its fields in place, then writes the old values to a separate undo log that readers consult for older snapshots.
PostgreSQL keeps a single copy of each row and uses row-level locks to block any transaction from reading a row while it is being updated, avoiding the need for multiple versions entirely.
Every UPDATE writes a new tuple version, but the old version is deleted immediately once the transaction commits, rather than being retained for older snapshots to see.

explanation: Specification answer: Every UPDATE writes a completely new tuple version to the heap page, populating xmin (creation transaction) and xmax (deletion transaction).

question: What is the purpose of the PostgreSQL Visibility Map? What is the purpose of the PostgreSQL Visibility Map?

options.text: It tracks which heap pages contain only tuples visible to all current transactions, allowing index-only scans to skip checking heap pages.
It tracks which heap pages have been modified since the last checkpoint, so WAL replay during crash recovery can skip pages that were never touched.
It stores a bitmap of which rows have been deleted but not yet vacuumed, so autovacuum can jump directly to pages containing dead tuples without scanning the whole table.
It records which pages are currently held in the shared buffer cache, allowing the planner to prefer index scans over sequential scans when a table is mostly cached in memory.

explanation: Specification answer: It tracks which heap pages contain only tuples visible to all current transactions, allowing index-only scans to skip checking heap pages.

question: What happens during a standard VACUUM vs VACUUM FULL? What happens during a standard VACUUM vs VACUUM FULL?

options.text: Standard VACUUM marks dead tuple space as reusable without shrinking file size; VACUUM FULL rewrites the table into a new file and reclaims disk space under an exclusive lock.
Standard VACUUM rewrites the table into a new file to reclaim disk space without locking, while VACUUM FULL only updates statistics for the query planner without touching dead tuples at all.
Standard VACUUM and VACUUM FULL both reclaim disk space identically; the only difference is that VACUUM FULL also runs ANALYZE afterward to refresh planner statistics.
Standard VACUUM deletes dead tuples permanently from the heap immediately, while VACUUM FULL merely marks them reusable for future inserts without shrinking the file.

explanation: Specification answer: Standard VACUUM marks dead tuple space as reusable without shrinking file size; VACUUM FULL rewrites the table into a new file and reclaims disk space under an exclusive lock.

question: Why does EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) provide more actionable insight than plain EXPLAIN? Why does EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) provide more actionable insight than plain EXPLAIN?

options.text: Plain EXPLAIN shows planner estimates; ANALYZE actually executes the query and reports real runtime, while BUFFERS shows exact shared buffer cache hits and disk reads.
ANALYZE only re-estimates the planner's row count guesses more precisely using sampled statistics, without actually executing the query at all.
BUFFERS reports the total size of the table and its indexes on disk, while ANALYZE shows which of several alternative query plans the optimizer considered.
Plain EXPLAIN already executes the query to get exact costs; ANALYZE and BUFFERS only add extra formatting to the same output, with no new information.

explanation: Specification answer: Plain EXPLAIN shows planner estimates; ANALYZE actually executes the query and reports real runtime, while BUFFERS shows exact shared buffer cache hits and disk reads.

question:
During triage in PostgreSQL MVCC Indexing EXPLAIN, an engineer observes:
"System fault during operation: Dead Tuple Bloat Prevents Autovacuum Reclamation".
What is the verified root cause?

options.text: A long-running reporting session opened a transaction with BEGIN; SELECT ... and remained idle in transaction for 18 hours, pinning xmin and preventing autovacuum from cleaning dead tuples.
A batch job runs VACUUM FULL on the table every night, but VACUUM FULL does not update the free space map, so the space it reclaims is never made available to new inserts.
autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor is set far too high for this table's size, so the threshold of dead tuples needed to trigger autovacuum is never reached even though no transaction is blocking it.

A replication slot on a standby server was never advanced after the standby was decommissioned, so PostgreSQL retains WAL segments indefinitely, which is mistaken for dead tuple bloat in the same monitoring dashboard.

explanation:
Root Cause: A long-running reporting session opened a transaction with BEGIN; SELECT ... and remained idle in transaction for 18 hours, pinning xmin and preventing autovacuum from cleaning dead tuples.

Fix Resolution:
Configure idleintransactionsessiontimeout = '60s' and terminate the lagging backend using SELECT pgterminatebackend(pid).
